\subsection{Cost and answer quality of each path}
\label{sec:res-paths}

\textbf{Takeaway: the page image alone is the strongest fixed policy; OCR text adds cost but little quality, and
retrieval misses dominate the errors.}
All three paths use the same generator (Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, greedy decoding). The text path reads the top-3
BM25 pages of OCR text; the visual path reads the top-1 ColPali page image (at most 1280 visual
tokens); the hybrid path reads both. Over all 8,150 questions, always-text reaches ANLS 0.367 at
0.43 GPU-s per query, always-visual 0.546 at 0.62 GPU-s, and always-hybrid
0.570 at 1.01 GPU-s (329\,J).
With a shared local generator the text path is therefore \emph{not} a cheap path:
OCR text costs about as many input tokens as a page image, and the text path is much less accurate.
The real cost differences are between one context and two (hybrid costs 1.6$\times$ the visual path and
2.3$\times$ the text path) and the size of the visual index at scale (Section~\ref{sec:res-scale}).
In 35\% of queries every path fails. For 76\% of these, no path had the gold page in its
context (page recall@1 is 0.44 for BM25 and 0.57 for ColPali; Table~\ref{tab:retrieval}). The two
retrievers miss different pages: the gold page is in the top 1 of either retriever for 0.64 of the
questions and in the top 3 of either for 0.74 (DocVQA 0.53 and 0.65,
InfographicVQA 0.84 and 0.92), and the hybrid path's context (three BM25 pages and the top
ColPali page) contains it for 0.68. No router
can recover the remaining queries from the retrieved contexts; they bound every policy that uses this retrieval.

Two controls on 1,500 of these questions (750 per dataset; Table~\ref{tab:controls}) show where the
differences between paths come from. First, the visual advantage is a matter of modality, not of how many pages
the generator reads: at equal depth, one page image beats one page of OCR text by 0.22 ANLS (95\% interval
0.194, 0.247), and three page images beat the three-page text path by 0.22 (0.189, 0.245), whereas going
from one page to three adds only 0.041 for text and 0.038 for images. Second, retrieval errors cost more
than any choice of path. Given the gold page, the visual path rises from 0.544 to 0.826, the text path
from 0.364 to 0.604 and the hybrid path from 0.556 to 0.839; the gain is largest on DocVQA
(+0.42 for the visual path, against +0.14 on InfographicVQA). Even with the gold page, the
image beats its OCR text by 0.22 ANLS (0.16 on DocVQA, 0.28 on InfographicVQA), and
adding the OCR text to the gold image adds only 0.013 (0.000, 0.024).

The path set and its input budgets matter for the cost comparison, so we placed the two depths outside it on the
same cost--quality plane, with generation times measured on the NVIDIA A10 (Table~\ref{tab:controls}; the three
paths' times are scaled by the A10-to-workstation ratio measured on the same questions). One page of OCR text
(559 input tokens) reaches ANLS 0.323 in 0.39\,s, against
0.364 in 0.84\,s for the three-page text path (1,556 tokens); three page images
(3,636 tokens) reach 0.582 in 3.29\,s, +0.026
[+0.008, +0.045] above the hybrid path at 1.96\,s. Of the five, only text top-1, the
visual path and visual top-3 lie on the upper convex hull of fixed policies; the three-page text path lies
0.119 ANLS below it and the hybrid path 0.004. At about the same input size, one page
image (1,251 tokens) beats three pages of text (1,556) by
+0.180 [+0.153, +0.208], so the advantage of the image does
not come from a larger budget. The evaluated path set is therefore not the efficient one: a per-query oracle over all
five contexts reaches ANLS 0.691 on these questions, against 0.634 over the three paths. Our routing
results hold for the three paths as defined; a router over a wider path set could do better, and the size of the
saving over always-hybrid depends on which expensive path it is measured against.

The image budget is itself a parameter of the visual and hybrid paths, so we re-ran both with the page image capped at
256, 512, 768 and 1,280 visual tokens (1,280 is the cap used everywhere else) on the same 1,500 control questions
on the NVIDIA A10 (Table~\ref{tab:token_sweep} in the Appendix). The visual path rises from ANLS 0.416
at 256 tokens to 0.544 at 1,280, and its generation time from 0.61 to 1.20\,s.
Even at 256 visual tokens (305 input tokens in all, 0.61\,s) it beats the three-page text
path (1,556 tokens, 0.95\,s) by +0.053 [+0.025, +0.079], so the image keeps its advantage
at a fifth of the text path's input. The text adds most when the image is small: the hybrid path beats the visual
path by +0.061 [+0.042, +0.081] at 256 tokens and by +0.011 [-0.005, +0.027] at 1,280
(+0.021 on DocVQA, +0.001 on InfographicVQA). DocVQA levels off near 768 tokens
(-0.005 [-0.015, +0.006] against 1,280) but InfographicVQA does not (-0.034
[-0.056, -0.014]), so a cap above 1,280 may still raise the visual path on infographics. It was not run: at
1,280 tokens the hybrid path already reserves up to 22.8\,GB of the A10's 24\,GB.

\subsection{Outcome-based route labels}
\label{sec:res-labels}

\textbf{Takeaway: keyword-rule labels agree with measured outcomes no better than chance.}
Route labels are derived from measured outcomes: the label of a query is the path that maximises
$\mathrm{ANLS} - \lambda \cdot \mathrm{cost}$, with ties broken towards the cheaper path (Table~\ref{tab:labels}).
Labels from a keyword rule over the question text agree with these outcome labels on 68.5\% of queries,
with Cohen's $\kappa = 0.01$, i.e.\ no agreement beyond chance; the keyword rule sends 97\% of
queries to the text path. On the 5,275 queries that at least one path answers, agreement falls to
52.7\% ($\kappa = 0.005$): most of the overall agreement comes from queries that every path
fails, which tie and default to the cheaper text path. Routing accuracy measured against keyword labels therefore says nothing about cost or answer
quality.

\subsection{Routing policies}
\label{sec:res-policies}

\textbf{Takeaway: reading the retrieved content, CAVR-CE saves 29\% of GPU compute against always-hybrid
at a small ANLS loss; against always-visual it gains a little for more compute.}
Table~\ref{tab:main_results} compares fixed policies, a keyword rule, simple learned baselines,
CAVR, the content-aware CAVR-CE and the per-query oracle. All router costs include the router's own measured
overhead and, where the router reads ColPali scores, ColPali retrieval for every query. Always-visual is the
strongest fixed policy per GPU-second, and always-hybrid the one that matches CAVR-CE's answer quality; we compare
the routers with both.

CAVR on question embeddings alone (ANLS 0.542 $\pm$ 0.014) shows no significant difference from always-visual:
on every seed the 95\% bootstrap interval of the ANLS difference includes zero and lies within
$\pm$0.007, while CAVR uses 4\% more GPU. The question text alone does not predict
which path will succeed.
CAVR-CE adds what is available before generation: an mpnet cross-encoder reads the question with the
best-matching OCR passages of the retrieved pages, plus retrieval scores and ColPali per-token match statistics.
With $\lambda$ chosen on each seed's validation split (the cheapest $\lambda$ within 0.005 ANLS of always-hybrid),
CAVR-CE reaches ANLS 0.557 $\pm$ 0.015 at 0.716 GPU-s per query, against
0.566 $\pm$ 0.020 at 1.009 GPU-s for always-hybrid: 29\% less GPU compute
(25--36\% across seeds; Table~\ref{tab:router_ce_tests}).
The price is a small ANLS loss: CAVR-CE is lower than always-hybrid on 4 of 5 seeds
(mean difference $-0.008$, range $-0.015$ to $+0.001$), and the 95\% bootstrap interval
excludes zero on 2 of 5 seeds. On exact match, McNemar's test finds no significant difference
on 5 of 5 seeds ($p = 0.098$--$0.74$), but with only 80--107
discordant pairs per seed it is underpowered, so this does not show that the two policies are equivalent.
Against always-visual, CAVR-CE gains $+0.012$ to $+0.018$ ANLS (bootstrap interval above zero on
5 of 5 seeds; McNemar on exact match $p \le 0.029$ on 5 of 5 seeds)
for 15\% more GPU.
Pooled over the five splits (a $t$ interval over splits, which is optimistic because the test sets overlap), the
ANLS difference to always-hybrid is -0.008 [-0.017, +0.000] and the saving 29\% [24, 35]; against
always-visual, CAVR-CE gains 0.016 [+0.013, +0.018] ANLS for 15\% [6, 25] more GPU compute.
Part of the saving over always-hybrid comes from using the hybrid path less often, whichever queries are chosen.
A quality-blind random mix of always-visual and always-hybrid at CAVR-CE's GPU cost reaches ANLS 0.547
(in expectation, computed per seed), and at CAVR-CE's ANLS it costs 0.896 GPU-s. The saving attributable
to choosing queries on these splits is therefore 20\% (13--26\% across seeds;
pooled interval [13, 27]\%), or $+0.010$ ANLS at equal cost. This saving was not confirmed on the held-out
set (Section~\ref{sec:res-confirm}), where always-visual dominates the mix.

The per-query oracle reaches ANLS 0.630 $\pm$ 0.016 at only 0.486 GPU-s, so substantial headroom
remains. It is limited by prediction: CAVR-CE predicts per-path success with a mean AUC of 0.842
(0.839 for gradient boosting on the same tabular features), and a learning curve over 25--100\% of the
training pages (2 seeds) rises only from 0.826 to 0.841. Run through the same decision rule,
gradient boosting on all of CAVR-CE's tabular features, including the ColPali token statistics, reaches ANLS 0.558 at 0.778 GPU-s: the same ANLS as CAVR-CE
(difference +0.000 [-0.006, +0.007]) but a 23\% rather than 29\% saving over always-hybrid
(no $\lambda$ reached the validation target on 5 of 5 splits, where the $\lambda$ with the highest
validation ANLS was used). Most of the gain therefore comes from the content features both predictors share; the
cross-encoder adds the remaining 2--10 points of saving across splits, measured at a
fallback operating point for gradient boosting.

How often does the router pick the oracle's path? Against the per-query oracle at the same $\lambda$, CAVR-CE's choice
is the same path on only 35\% of test queries, but on 89\% of queries several paths reach the best
ANLS (on 35\% all of them fail), and the oracle then takes the cheapest, usually the text path; the router's
path reaches the query's best ANLS on 91\% of queries. In the confusion matrix (Table~\ref{tab:confusion},
Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix}), the largest off-diagonal cell is the 60\% of the router's visual choices
for which the oracle takes the cheaper text path, mostly because both fail or both succeed; this is where the oracle's
remaining saving lies. Charging each query the GPU memory it holds rather than
its GPU time alone, as peak reserved memory (16.4--17.9\,GiB, mostly model weights) times
GPU-seconds, does not change the comparison: CAVR-CE holds 11.7\,GiB$\cdot$s per query, against 18.1 for
always-hybrid (35\% less) and 10.2 for always-visual (15\% more). The evaluation index
(0.44\,GiB) is resident for every policy.

Where does routing gain over always-visual? On DocVQA, CAVR-CE is +0.017 [+0.012, +0.022] ANLS
above it and on InfographicVQA +0.012 [+0.002, +0.022] (intervals over splits). The gain is
concentrated where the OCR text helps to read the answer: tables and lists (+0.027
[+0.021, +0.033]) and free text (+0.029 [+0.005, +0.052]) on DocVQA,
whereas on layout and figure questions the interval includes zero (+0.004 and
+0.007). Even where it helps, a path with OCR text
beats the page image alone on only 9\% of DocVQA and 16\% of InfographicVQA
questions, so the possible gain over the best single path is small, and it depends on how often such questions
occur.

\subsection{Held-out confirmation}
\label{sec:res-confirm}

\textbf{Takeaway: on new questions the saving over always-hybrid persists; a gain over always-visual does not.}
The router was designed on the same five splits that we report on. To test it on questions that played no part in
its design, each seed's CAVR-CE was re-trained with the same code, training split, hyperparameters and seed on the
NVIDIA A10 node (the main run's weights were not stored), kept its validation-chosen $\lambda$ and training-split
cost estimates, and was applied without any tuning to 1,499 new questions from the
DocVQA and InfographicVQA training splits (1,097 pages, none shared with the validation data;
Section~\ref{sec:setup-confirm}). The re-trained routers make the same choice as the saved ones on
80--93\% of their original test queries, with test ANLS within $\pm$0.007.

On the confirmation set (Table~\ref{tab:confirmation}), the saving over always-hybrid holds. CAVR-CE reaches ANLS
0.605 (0.600--0.609 across seeds) at 1.32 GPU-s per query, against 0.590 at
2.03 GPU-s for always-hybrid: 35\% less GPU compute (31--44\%), with ANLS
higher by 0.014 rather than lower (bootstrap interval above zero on 3 of 5 seeds; McNemar
$p < 0.05$ in CAVR-CE's favour on 4 of 5). The gain over the best fixed path does not carry over.
On these questions the hybrid path is less accurate than the visual path (0.590 against 0.600),
so always-visual is the best fixed policy: CAVR-CE exceeds it by only 0.005 ANLS (interval includes zero on
4 of 5 seeds) and uses 19\% more GPU compute. A quality-blind mix of the visual and
hybrid paths is then dominated by always-visual, so the query-selection saving of Section~\ref{sec:res-policies} is
not confirmed on this set. GPU-seconds here are measured on the NVIDIA A10, about 2.0$\times$ slower per
query than the workstation, so they are comparable within the set but not with Table~\ref{tab:main_results}.
Averaged over the five re-trained routers, with one page-cluster bootstrap over the 1,097 pages, CAVR-CE is
+0.014 [+0.005, +0.024] ANLS above always-hybrid at 35\% [34, 36] less GPU compute, and
+0.005 [-0.004, +0.014] above always-visual at 19\% [18, 21] more.

These questions come from the datasets' training splits. ColPali's training data include the DocVQA and
InfographicVQA training sets~\cite{colpali}; we could not establish from public documentation whether the generator
saw them. Two diagnostics point to such exposure. On DocVQA, when the gold page was not in the context, training-split questions
still scored higher than validation questions on every path (visual 0.26 against
0.11, hybrid 0.20 against 0.09, text 0.10 against
0.06, reweighted to the validation mix of question types). Memorised answers would produce this, and
so would answers repeated on a retrieved sibling page of the same document. On InfographicVQA, with the gold page in
context, the visual path scored 0.93 on training-split questions against 0.75 on
validation questions (its training split carries no question types to reweight by). The confirmation set therefore
tests the routers on new questions, but not on unseen data: the higher accuracy of the visual path there, and
with it the reversal of the visual and hybrid paths, may partly reflect exposure. We take from it only the
qualitative findings: the saving over always-hybrid persists, although its size may also be affected, and a gain
over always-visual is not established. Per dataset, CAVR-CE is +0.003 [-0.008, +0.013] ANLS from always-visual
on DocVQA and +0.007 [-0.007, +0.022] on InfographicVQA; a path with OCR text beats the page image alone on only
8\% and 8\% of these questions (9\% and 16\% of the
validation test questions), which leaves routing less to gain.

\subsection{Runtime budget control}
\label{sec:res-lambda}

\textbf{Takeaway: one trained router covers a range of budgets by changing $\lambda$ alone.}
The decision rule $\arg\max_p \hat{q}_p - \lambda c_p$ takes the cost weight $\lambda$ as an input, so one trained
router covers a range of budgets without retraining; $\lambda$ is a per-deployment setting, chosen from the
operating points below for a target quality or capacity. Its cost estimates are specific to the hardware and serving
stack, so a new deployment should re-measure the per-path costs before choosing $\lambda$. Sweeping $\lambda$ from 1 to 0 moves CAVR-CE from
ANLS 0.502 at 0.56 GPU-s to 0.564 at 0.84 GPU-s (mean over seeds;
Figure~\ref{fig:pareto} shows seed 1). Table~\ref{tab:load_test_ops} gives the serving capacity of each operating
point on seed 1.

  per-query oracle. Costs are measured GPU-seconds per query including router overhead.}

\subsection{Confidence-based escalation}
\label{sec:res-escalation}

\textbf{Takeaway: escalation is not an independent improvement; lowering $\lambda$ reaches the same operating points.}
Escalation sends a query to the hybrid path when a calibrated probability that its routed answer is good falls
below $\tau$ (Table~\ref{tab:escalation}, Figure~\ref{fig:escalation}). Probabilities are calibrated on the
validation split by logistic regression; their expected calibration error on test is 0.027--0.078
depending on the signal. On top of CAVR-CE, re-routing on the ColPali score margin at $\tau = 0.5$ raises ANLS
from 0.557 to 0.564 and GPU cost from 0.716 to 0.856 GPU-s
(34\% of queries escalated), still 15\% below always-hybrid.
Setting $\lambda = 0$ reaches the same point without escalation (ANLS 0.564 at 0.845 GPU-s), and
the signal and $\tau$ shown here were highlighted after inspecting test results, so this comparison is exploratory.
Comparing every escalation operating point (all signals, $\tau$ from 0.3 to 0.9) with the frontier that sweeping
$\lambda$ traces at the same mean GPU cost, escalation is on average -0.002 ANLS from that frontier and at best
0.005 above it (at most 0.010 on any split); 26\% of its points lie above it, all by less than
the split-to-split variation. Escalation therefore does not improve the cost--quality trade-off beyond what the cost
weight already provides; we report it as a negative result, and its use is limited to deployments that need an
explicit confidence threshold rather than a cost weight.
Because the re-routing decision is made before generation, it adds no serial step, and its latency cost is small:
p95 latency rises from 1.24\,s to 1.36\,s, against 1.39\,s for always-hybrid. Signals
that judge the generated answer (token log-probabilities) can be computed only after the routed answer exists. Computed from the measured
per-stage times, a serial cascade has p95 1.91\,s; launching the hybrid path alongside the routed path cuts
p95 to 1.42\,s but costs 1.46 GPU-s per query, 45\% more than always-hybrid (assuming two
concurrent workers).

\subsection{Scalability, throughput and energy}
\label{sec:res-scale}

\textbf{Takeaway: measured live, routing keeps its advantage over always-hybrid under load; the simulator keeps the
order of the policies but overestimates capacity, so its GPU counts for large pools are projections.}
The live measurements come first and carry the comparison; the simulation projects them to larger pools.

\paragraph{Live serving on two A10 GPUs.} To test the simulator, we served the generation stage live with
vLLM on one and two A10 GPUs (Table~\ref{tab:live_serving}, Figure~\ref{fig:live_serving}). The served model
closely reproduced the cached run. All 150 pilot prompts had the same token count as on the workstation; over the
4,818 service-time requests (1,606 queries on each path), path ANLS differed from the workstation run by at
most 0.003, and 96--98\% of answers were identical. With one request at a time, an
A10 took 0.52, 0.59 and 0.88\,s per text, visual and hybrid request, against
0.44, 0.58 and 0.96\,s of generation on the workstation.

Under Poisson load the policies kept the order the simulation gives, and routing gained more than simulated. At
p95 $\le$ 5\,s, CAVR-CE sustained 1.86$\times$ the arrival rate of always-hybrid on one GPU and
1.82$\times$ on two, where the simulator, given the A10's own service times and batching curve,
predicted 1.46$\times$ and 1.62$\times$. On two GPUs at p95 $\le$ 2\,s the ratio was
2.82 (simulated 2.13). Always-visual remained ahead of CAVR-CE, which sustained
0.87$\times$ and 0.90$\times$ its rate at 5\,s, as in the simulation. Answer
quality did not change under load: ANLS over the tested rates was 0.567 for CAVR-CE, 0.573 for
always-hybrid and 0.542 for always-visual on two GPUs, close to the workstation's ANLS on the same requests.
At each policy's highest tested rate, CAVR-CE used 74\,J of GPU energy per request, against 111\,J for
always-hybrid (33\% less) and 65\,J for always-visual.

Absolute capacity, by contrast, was lower than simulated. At p95 $\le$ 5\,s the simulator predicted
1.4--2.0$\times$ the measured capacity, and on the measured arrival traces its p95 was off by a
median of 37--57\% per run; inputs from the workstation gave similar predictions. At
p95 $\le$ 2\,s, one A10 met the target only with always-visual, up to 0.37 queries/s, where the simulator
predicted 1.06. The test points to two effects that the simulator leaves out. First, at the lowest rate a
request that reached an idle replica took 1.22--1.37$\times$ the time the same request took back to
back with others; GPU clocks dropping between requests are a likely cause. Second, vLLM batches continuously: the
prefill of a new request (on average 1,265 prompt tokens on the visual path and 2,675 on the
hybrid path, while answers average at most 6 tokens) runs alongside the requests already in progress
and slows them down, whereas the simulator treats a batch as uninterrupted once it starts. Adding a second GPU raised
the measured capacity at 5\,s by 2.7--2.8$\times$, more than the
2.1--2.4$\times$ predicted, which is consistent with the larger pooling gain of a shared
dispatcher when service times vary more than the model assumes. The simulated GPU counts of Table~\ref{tab:load_test} are therefore reported as simulated: on one and two A10
GPUs the simulator overestimated capacity at p95 $\le$ 5\,s by 1.4--2.0$\times$, the
error was smaller with two GPUs than with one, and how it changes with pool size beyond two GPUs is not known. At
2\,s the error was larger: on one A10, CAVR-CE and always-hybrid missed the target even at the lowest tested rate. The order of the policies
and CAVR-CE's advantage over always-hybrid held in the live test.

\paragraph{Serving under load (simulated projection).} A Poisson load test with dynamic batching, simulated from the measured per-query
service times and measured batching curves, gives the highest arrival rate one GPU sustains at p95 $\le$ 2\,s and
the number of GPUs needed for a given load (Table~\ref{tab:load_test}, mean over seeds; Figure~\ref{fig:gpus},
seed 1). Serving 100 queries/s at p95 $\le$ 2\,s needs 106.0 $\pm$ 0.7 GPUs for always-hybrid,
72.4 $\pm$ 4.4 for CAVR-CE (32\% fewer), 64.4 $\pm$ 0.5 for always-visual and
41.6 $\pm$ 0.9 for the oracle. At this target batches rarely form: the ratio of GPUs needed by CAVR-CE and always-hybrid (0.68)
tracks their ratio of batch-1 GPU-seconds (0.71). The saving depends on the target, as the sweep below shows. With HF Transformers
generation (no serving engine such as vLLM~\cite{vllm}), one GPU serves at most 3.88 (text), 3.06
(visual) and 1.80 (hybrid) queries/s at the best batch size within memory. The simulation keeps the
evaluation index (1,786 pages) on every GPU; routing saves generation compute, not index memory, because
CAVR-CE reads ColPali scores for every query.
Across p95 targets from 1.5 to 10\,s, on all five splits, CAVR-CE needs 22--32\%
fewer GPUs than always-hybrid and 10--16\% more than always-visual (Table~\ref{tab:slo_sweep}).
The simulator charges a batch the mean generation time of its members, scaled by the measured batching curve;
charging the longest member instead, a conservative bound, the saving over always-hybrid is 30\% at 2\,s and
15\% at 5\,s (against 24\% with the mean member).

\paragraph{Generation and retrieval together.} The load test keeps the small evaluation index on every GPU. For a
large corpus, a retrieval tier is needed as well. Projected from the workstation's measured MaxSim throughput at
batch 64, scaled linearly in pages and at full utilisation, 100 queries/s over a million pages needs 20 GPUs
for retrieval (14 just to hold the index) for every policy that reads ColPali on every query. CAVR-CE then
needs 92 GPUs in total, against 126 for always-hybrid and 84 for always-visual. The question-only
router could skip ColPali for the queries it sends to the text path, but it sends only 2\% there and
needs 84 GPUs. Routing thus saves the same number of generation GPUs at any corpus size, while the index
adds a cost that every visual policy pays.

\paragraph{Load-adaptive $\lambda$.} On a fixed pool of 74 GPUs, the number CAVR-CE needs for 100 queries/s
at p95 $\le$ 2\,s, arrivals alternate between 80 queries/s for 60\,s and 140 queries/s for
20\,s (split 1). CAVR-CE at its validation-chosen $\lambda$ answers 77.5\% of requests within 2\,s
(ANLS 0.560); always-hybrid manages 34.8\%. A controller that raises $\lambda$ when the oldest
queued request has waited longer than a threshold (chosen on validation queries) moves 18\% of requests to a
higher $\lambda$ and reaches 80.1\% (ANLS 0.559), whereas a fixed $\lambda = 0.2$ reaches
88.3\% (ANLS 0.551) and always-visual 88.7\%. This is a negative result: the controller
is worse than simply fixing a higher $\lambda$. In this simulator overload appears mostly as
larger and slower batches rather than long queues, so a queue-driven controller reacts little; adapting $\lambda$
to load would need a better overload signal, such as GPU busy time, which we leave open.

\paragraph{Visual index scaling.} ColPali stores 1,031 vectors per page. At 100k pages the index needs
24.6\,GiB in bf16, more than our 24\,GiB GPU holds before any model weights or activations, and a
million pages (about 246\,GiB) would exceed the memory of most current accelerators
(Table~\ref{tab:index_scaling}, Figure~\ref{fig:index}). Streaming it from pinned host memory costs
1,044\,ms per query; 2$\times$2 pooling shrinks it to 6.3\,GiB and 10.3\,ms
but lowers recall@1 on the real corpus from 0.577 to 0.525 (both measured with the same batched
query encoding). Hierarchical token pooling~\cite{tokenpooling}, which clusters each page's patch vectors and keeps
one mean vector per cluster, does much better at the same size: with 263 vectors per page it keeps recall@1 at 0.574 and recall@5 at
0.747, against 0.578 and 0.751 for the full index and 0.525 and 0.712 for 2$\times$2
pooling (Table~\ref{tab:token_pooling}). A 3.9$\times$ smaller index makes a million pages 63\,GiB,
which 5 A10s could hold, and scoring cost falls in proportion to the vectors per page. Emulated sharding over
2 GPUs (shards timed one after another on this GPU) gives
19.8\,ms. A GPU-resident index answers in 0.55\,ms at 1k pages and 19.8\,ms at
50k pages.

\paragraph{Offline cost.} Building a 100k-page index would take about 1.7 GPU-hours, extrapolated from a 64-page
benchmark at batch 4 (16.2 pages/s); the 1,786-page evaluation index was built at batch
8, which exceeded GPU memory, and ran at 11.3 pages per GPU-second. docTR OCR of the
1,786 evaluation pages took 471\,s and 29.3\,kJ.

\paragraph{Multi-GPU index sharding.} Exhaustive MaxSim is embarrassingly parallel over pages, so near-linear
scaling is the expected outcome; what the measurement adds is how close to linear it comes and what dispatching
queries and merging per-shard results cost within one node. On the three-GPU node (Table~\ref{tab:multi_gpu},
Figure~\ref{fig:multi_gpu}), sharded search returned the same top page as one GPU for all 500 check questions
(99.8\% exactly, the rest exact score ties). Latency is set by the number of pages per GPU. A 50k-page index is
searched in 327\,ms on one GPU, 164\,ms on two and 109\,ms on three (speedup
2.99$\times$); from 50k pages up, parallel efficiency is at least 99.6\% and dispatch and merge
add at most 0.6\,ms over an ideal split. Throughput at batch 64 scales by the same factor, with
efficiency of at least 99.7\% from 10k pages up. With 50k pages per GPU, a
150k-page index of 36.9\,GiB, larger than the memory of any one GPU on the node, is searched in
328\,ms, as fast as 50k pages on one GPU (weak-scaling efficiency 99.9\%). Smaller
corpora gain less at batch 1 (three GPUs give 2.51$\times$ at 1k pages and 2.52$\times$ at 10k pages),
where per-query overheads are a larger share of a short search; their batch-64 throughput still reaches
96\% and 102\% of linear scaling.

Energy per query for the whole node falls from
28.4\,J on one GPU to 17.8\,J on three at 50k pages, but not because the GPUs work more efficiently: an
unused GPU, which holds a CUDA context in the benchmark process, draws about 51\,W (estimated from the runs; 50--53\,W across
configurations), and without the idle draw the active energy is 17.8\,J per query whatever the number of GPUs.
On a node whose GPUs are powered anyway, spreading the shards over all of them therefore lowers the energy per query.
These GPUs are much slower than the workstation's: one Tesla P40 takes 327\,ms for the 50k-page search that
the RTX 4090 completes in 19.8\,ms in bf16, 17$\times$ faster. Absolute times therefore do not
transfer between the machines; the scaling with the number of GPUs does. It also shows that the emulated sharding above
omitted little: merging the shard results costs well under a millisecond.

\paragraph{Sharding on data-centre GPUs.} The same benchmark, unchanged, ran on a node with two
NVIDIA A10 GPUs (Ampere, scored in fp16; Table~\ref{tab:hardware_multigpu}). Sharded search again returned the same
top page as one GPU for all 500 check questions (99.8\% exactly, the rest exact score ties). A
50k-page index is searched in 41.1\,ms on one A10 and 21.0\,ms on two (parallel efficiency
97.6\%); from 50k pages up, dispatch and merge add at most 0.5\,ms, and batch-64
throughput efficiency is at least 98.6\% from 10k pages up. A 100k-page index
(24.6\,GiB, more than one A10 holds) is searched in 41.4\,ms on two GPUs, as fast as
50k pages on one (weak-scaling efficiency 99.2\%), and the largest corpus run on two A10s,
120k pages, took 49.5\,ms. One A10 is 8$\times$ faster than one P40 on the 50k-page search and uses
5.6$\times$ less active energy per query (3.2 against 17.8\,J), largely because it
scores in fp16 on tensor cores, which the P40 lacks; it is still 2.1$\times$ slower than the RTX 4090.
As on the P40 node, active energy per query does not depend on the number of GPUs (3.2 and
3.2\,J at 50k pages). Near-linear sharding therefore holds across two GPU generations and two scoring
precisions; the parallel efficiency transfers between machines, the absolute speed does not.

\paragraph{Host-memory placement at a million pages.} With the index held in host memory, two NVIDIA A10 GPUs
searched a million pages (246\,GiB). Held in GPU memory within the same 70\% per-GPU budget
(15.6\,GiB), this index would need 16 A10s, or 8 nodes like this one
(Table~\ref{tab:host_stream}, Figure~\ref{fig:host_stream}). Streamed search returned the same top page, up to the
repetition of real pages in the corpus, and the same score as GPU-resident search for all 100 check questions
on 100k pages. Single queries were bound by the PCIe link: their latency stayed within 4\% of
the time needed to copy each GPU's shard, and at a million pages it was 10.9\,s on one GPU and
6.4\,s on two. The workstation shows the same bound, streaming 100k pages from host memory in
1,044\,ms against 1.10\,s on one A10. One A10 read host memory at 24.2\,GB/s and two
together at 41.0\,GB/s, 85\% of twice the single-GPU rate, so a second GPU cut single-query latency by
only 1.7$\times$. The cause of this shortfall was not identified: nvidia-smi reports a path through several PCIe
bridges between the two GPUs, and the placement of host memory across the two CPU sockets was not controlled.

Batching removes the PCIe bound, because one pass over the index serves every query in the batch. Scoring rather than
copying sets the pace from about 25--30 queries per batch, a crossover derived from the batch-1 and
batch-64 times on the assumption that scoring time grows linearly with batch size. At batch 64 and
a million pages, throughput was 2.25 queries/s on one GPU and 4.50 on two (2.0$\times$),
or 0.44\,GPU-s per query; GPU-resident search would cost about 0.43\,GPU-s, scaled linearly from
its 100k-page run. Where both placements were measured on the same corpus (100k pages, two GPUs),
streamed search reached 94\% of the GPU-resident throughput at batch 64 with a GPU energy of
6.7 against 6.4\,J per query; the host CPU and memory energy that streaming adds was not measured.
At batch 1 the comparison reverses: streamed search used 1.29 against 0.083\,GPU-s and
99 against 15\,J per query. Host-memory placement therefore trades latency for GPU count at about
the same throughput per GPU, but only for workloads that fill large batches. At 6.4\,s per single query and
about 14\,s per batch of 64, it misses the 2\,s p95 target of the load test and suits batch or offline
search. Interactive search over a million pages needs GPU-resident sharding, projected at about
51\,ms on 16 A10s (linear fit of the resident runs against pages per GPU, without the cost of
merging results across nodes), or a compressed index.

\paragraph{Router overhead.} The CAVR router (mpnet embedding and MLP) takes 11.7\,ms per query at
batch 1 on the GPU (25.0\,ms on the CPU) and reaches 12,454 queries/s at large
batch. CAVR-CE takes 24.8\,ms and 1.74\,J per query at batch 1, and its cross-encoder sustains
389 queries/s. Neither is a bottleneck next to generation (Table~\ref{tab:router_throughput}).

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:res-limits}

All experiments ran within a single node: the cached run of every path, router training and evaluation on one
consumer GPU (GeForce RTX 4090) under Windows, and the controls, confirmation set, live serving, index sharding and host-memory
index on the server nodes of Table~\ref{tab:hardware_multigpu}, with at most three GPUs per node. No
multi-node experiment was run, so interconnect traffic, distributed merging of shard results and cross-node scheduling
are not measured, and statements about larger clusters are projections. Caps on visual tokens and OCR length keep memory
below the point where the driver spills to system RAM. The cached run generates with HF Transformers. The 2\,s latency target is our choice; the saving is smaller at looser targets.

The workstation load test is a simulation driven by measured service times. Checked against live vLLM serving on one
and two A10 GPUs, it overestimated capacity at p95 $\le$ 5\,s by 1.4--2.0$\times$, and
by more at 2\,s, so its GPU counts are simulated estimates whose error beyond two GPUs is unknown; the live test kept
the order of the policies at 5\,s. Each live rate is a single arrival trace, so the live capacities carry no
interval. That test serves
generation only, with retrieval and routing run beforehand, on at most two GPUs under WSL, with one model and
greedy decoding. Escalation latencies are
computed from measured per-stage times rather than measured on concurrent workers. The simulator assumes an ideal
global queue and unlimited CPU, charges a batch the mean generation time of its members (the longest-member bound is reported), and keeps the
1,786-page evaluation index on every GPU, so the retrieval tier for a large corpus is projected rather than simulated. Retrieval
searches each dataset's whole page pool with questions written for a single page, so page recall@1 is only
0.57 for ColPali (Section~\ref{sec:res-paths}); how many misses come from questions that do not identify their
page was not annotated. The image-token sweep stops at the cap of 1,280 visual tokens used throughout, where
InfographicVQA had not levelled off (Section~\ref{sec:res-paths}); a higher budget may raise the visual and hybrid
paths on infographics, so the comparison of the paths on InfographicVQA holds for this cap. The
confirmation set comes from training splits the generator and ColPali may have seen (Section~\ref{sec:res-confirm}).
Costs
are measured without prefix or encoder caching, which would favour paths whose page image repeats across
questions. Indexes of 10k--1M pages
repeat the real page embeddings, which is valid for latency and memory but not for retrieval quality at that
scale; the recall of pooled indexes is measured on the 1,786 real pages only. Multi-GPU sharding was measured for retrieval only, on two server nodes with at most three GPUs
each (Tesla P40, NVIDIA A10), whose absolute times do not transfer to the workstation, and the load test does not include sharded retrieval. The host-memory index was measured in one process on one node, with 5 latency queries and 2
repetitions per batch (latency varied by at most 0.5\% within the run) and with host memory placed across CPU
sockets without control, and GPU-resident search at a million pages is
projected from smaller resident runs, not measured.

Energy covers the GPU only (NVML); host CPU and memory energy is not counted. Answers are short (at most
32 tokens), so cost is dominated by processing the input; with longer answers the relative cost of an
extra context shrinks. The savings are relative to this path set and one shared generator, and they depend on the
retrieval depth and input caps of each path. The path set is not the efficient one: on the 1,500 control
questions, one page of OCR text and three page images lie on the cost--quality frontier where the three-page text
path and the hybrid path do not (Section~\ref{sec:res-paths}); routers over that wider set were not trained, because
those contexts were run only on the control sample. Routing to a smaller generator was not tested. The router handles text
queries over visual documents; queries that contain an image are out of scope. The router design was developed on the same five splits that we
report on, and the feasibility analyses that motivated it looked at their test portions; no parameter of the final
pipeline is selected on test data. On a held-out confirmation set, the saving over always-hybrid held but the
gain over always-visual did not (Section~\ref{sec:res-confirm}): which fixed path is best, and so what routing
gains over it, depends on the question distribution. The confirmation questions come from the training splits of
the same two datasets and were run on a different GPU, so they test new questions and pages, not new datasets, and
no data set with documented non-exposure of ColPali and the generator was evaluated. The routers applied to them
were re-trained with the same recipe rather than reloaded, which is not bit-exact. Splits group
questions by page, so pages of one DocVQA document can fall into different splits. Finally, the 35\% of
queries that every path fails bound what routing can achieve on this benchmark.
